title: Claude Mythos 5 Beats Most Efficient Quantum Circuits on 7 of 8 Tasks
summary:
Anthropic's newest AI model improved the efficiency of quantum circuits by an order of magnitude or more across multiple computational primitives. Using Claude Mythos 5, researchers created designs that required fewer qubits and Toffoli gates than previous benchmarks on seven of eight tested tasks. The model operated in a closed loop, proposing architectures and using feedback from an independent evaluator program to refine designs without human intervention.

The project was a collaboration with Harvard and other researchers using the OpenEvolve tool to search circuit-generating programs for applications in chemistry, materials science, and number theory. In one instance, the AI developed the first reversible implementation of divsteps, a classical algorithm that was previously impractical for reversible arithmetic, by deriving new algebraic identities and formalizing the claim in Lean. These efficiencies reduce the hardware resources needed for quantum algorithms, which could accelerate the viability of quantum computing applications.

selectedTweets.text:
Banger paper from Anthropic, Harvard, and colleagues.

They find that LLM-proposed quantum circuits beat the best-known designs on seven of eight tasks, with fewer Toffoli gates and fewer qubits.

They search over these circuit-generating programs with OpenEvolve, using Claude Mythos 5 to propose architectures and program rewrites.

LLMs propose circuit designs, an independent evaluator verifies correctness and scores the cost, and the best designs seed the next round.

The tasks cover numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory.

On the eighth task, the search found a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. It makes divsteps, a classical algorithm impractical for reversible arithmetic, usable and improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off.

The evaluator verifies every circuit before scoring, so each reported gain is a checked circuit.

selectedTweets.bestBit: Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history
selectedTweets.text:
'Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.'
